items.title: I can give reasons why substances need to move through the plasma membrane
items.what: Cells need nutrients (water, oxygen, amino acids, glucose, lipids, ions) to carry out essential processes such as growth, repair and reproduction. Cells also need to remove waste products (carbon dioxide, urea, excess water) to prevent toxic build-up.
items.why: Understanding why transport occurs gives context to all the specific transport mechanisms. Without this movement, a cell would run out of reactants or be poisoned by its own waste.
items.example: A muscle cell during exercise needs a constant supply of oxygen and glucose for cellular respiration, and must rapidly remove carbon dioxide. If CO2 accumulates, the cell's pH drops and enzymes stop functioning.

subtopic.name: Transport pathways
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the different types of substances that cross the plasma membrane and the modes of transport they use. It distinguishes between passive transport (simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion) and active transport (protein pumps, bulk transport), and links each mode to the structural component of the membrane involved.
subtopic.why: Understanding how and why substances move across the plasma membrane is central to explaining how cells survive. This knowledge underpins later topics on osmosis, cellular respiration and body systems.

items.title: I can define semi-permeable, hydrophilic and hydrophobic
items.what: Semi-permeable means allowing some substances to pass through while preventing the movement of others. Hydrophilic means dissolving easily in water (also called lipophobic). Hydrophobic means not dissolving readily in water (also called lipophilic).
items.why: These terms explain why different substances use different transport routes. The nature of the substance determines whether it can pass through the phospholipid bilayer or needs a protein channel.
items.example: Oxygen is a small non-polar molecule, so it is hydrophobic and passes directly through the phospholipid bilayer. Glucose is hydrophilic and polar, so it cannot cross the bilayer and instead requires a carrier protein.

subtopic.name: Transport pathways
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the different types of substances that cross the plasma membrane and the modes of transport they use. It distinguishes between passive transport (simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion) and active transport (protein pumps, bulk transport), and links each mode to the structural component of the membrane involved.
subtopic.why: Understanding how and why substances move across the plasma membrane is central to explaining how cells survive. This knowledge underpins later topics on osmosis, cellular respiration and body systems.

items.title: I can distinguish between passive transport and active transport
items.what: Passive transport moves substances from high to low concentration without energy input (ATP). It includes simple diffusion, osmosis and facilitated diffusion. Active transport moves substances from low to high concentration and requires ATP. It includes active transport via protein pumps and bulk transport (endocytosis and exocytosis).
items.why: Classifying transport as passive or active is fundamental to understanding how cells regulate their internal environment. It also explains why cells need energy from cellular respiration.
items.example: Oxygen enters a cell by simple diffusion (passive, no ATP needed, high to low concentration). Sodium ions are pumped out of a neuron by the sodium-potassium pump (active, requires ATP, low to high concentration).

subtopic.name: Transport pathways
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the different types of substances that cross the plasma membrane and the modes of transport they use. It distinguishes between passive transport (simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion) and active transport (protein pumps, bulk transport), and links each mode to the structural component of the membrane involved.
subtopic.why: Understanding how and why substances move across the plasma membrane is central to explaining how cells survive. This knowledge underpins later topics on osmosis, cellular respiration and body systems.

items.title: I can summarise simple diffusion including the substances involved, energy requirements and membrane component used
items.what: Simple diffusion is the net passive movement of a substance from a region of high concentration to a region of low concentration until equilibrium is reached. It requires no energy and occurs through the phospholipid bilayer. Substances that move this way include oxygen, carbon dioxide, urea, alcohol and steroid hormones.
items.why: Simple diffusion is the most basic transport mechanism and occurs in both living and non-living systems. Understanding it provides the foundation for understanding all other transport types.
items.example: Carbon dioxide is produced as a waste product of cellular respiration inside the cell. Because its concentration is higher inside the cell than outside, it diffuses out through the phospholipid bilayer without any energy input.

subtopic.name: Transport pathways
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the different types of substances that cross the plasma membrane and the modes of transport they use. It distinguishes between passive transport (simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion) and active transport (protein pumps, bulk transport), and links each mode to the structural component of the membrane involved.
subtopic.why: Understanding how and why substances move across the plasma membrane is central to explaining how cells survive. This knowledge underpins later topics on osmosis, cellular respiration and body systems.

items.title: I can summarise facilitated diffusion including the substances involved, energy requirements and membrane component used
items.what: Facilitated diffusion is the net passive movement of hydrophilic or polar substances from high to low concentration with the assistance of channel proteins or carrier proteins. It requires no energy. Carrier proteins bind to a specific substance and change shape to move it across. Channel proteins allow substances to pass through a pore.
items.why: Many essential substances like glucose and amino acids are hydrophilic and cannot cross the phospholipid bilayer directly. Facilitated diffusion explains how these substances enter or leave cells without energy expenditure.
items.example: Glucose enters a red blood cell via a carrier protein called a uniporter. The carrier protein binds glucose on one side of the membrane, changes shape, and releases it on the other side. No ATP is used because glucose moves down its concentration gradient.

subtopic.name: Transport pathways
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the different types of substances that cross the plasma membrane and the modes of transport they use. It distinguishes between passive transport (simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion) and active transport (protein pumps, bulk transport), and links each mode to the structural component of the membrane involved.
subtopic.why: Understanding how and why substances move across the plasma membrane is central to explaining how cells survive. This knowledge underpins later topics on osmosis, cellular respiration and body systems.

items.title: I can summarise active transport including the substances involved, energy requirements and membrane component used
items.what: Active transport is the net movement of a substance from a region of low concentration to a region of high concentration using a carrier protein (protein pump) and ATP. It is selective, meaning the carrier proteins are specific to certain substances. A well-known example is the sodium-potassium pump in neurons.
items.why: Active transport allows cells to maintain internal concentrations that differ from the external environment, which is essential for processes like nerve impulse transmission and nutrient absorption in the small intestine.
items.example: The sodium-potassium pump in a neuron moves 3 Na+ ions out of the cell and 2 K+ ions into the cell, both against their concentration gradients. This requires ATP and creates the charge difference needed for nerve impulses.

subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the different types of substances that cross the plasma membrane and the modes of transport they use. It distinguishes between passive transport (simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion) and active transport (protein pumps, bulk transport), and links each mode to the structural component of the membrane involved.
subtopic.why: Understanding how and why substances move across the plasma membrane is central to explaining how cells survive. This knowledge underpins later topics on osmosis, cellular respiration and body systems.

items.title: I can describe bulk transport including endocytosis and exocytosis
items.what: Bulk transport moves large particles or large volumes of liquid across the plasma membrane using vesicles and ATP. Endocytosis brings substances into the cell by engulfing them in a vesicle formed from the plasma membrane. Exocytosis exports substances by fusing a vesicle with the plasma membrane. Phagocytosis is endocytosis of solids; pinocytosis is endocytosis of liquids.
items.why: Some substances are too large to pass through the phospholipid bilayer or protein channels. Bulk transport explains how cells take in food particles, export proteins, and dispose of pathogens.
items.example: A white blood cell engulfs a bacterium by phagocytosis: the plasma membrane surrounds the bacterium, pinches off to form a vesicle inside the cell, and the bacterium is then broken down by enzymes in a lysosome.

subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the different types of substances that cross the plasma membrane and the modes of transport they use. It distinguishes between passive transport (simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion) and active transport (protein pumps, bulk transport), and links each mode to the structural component of the membrane involved.

items.title: I can summarise the process of osmosis including the substance moving, energy requirements and membrane component involved
items.what: Osmosis is the net passive movement of free water from a region of high free water concentration to a region of low free water concentration across a semi-permeable membrane until equilibrium is reached. It requires no energy (ATP). Water moves through the phospholipid bilayer via pores. An alternative definition refers to movement from low solute concentration to high solute concentration.
items.why: Osmosis is a special case of diffusion that applies specifically to water. Since water is the medium for most cellular reactions, understanding how it moves is critical to understanding cell function and survival.
items.example: If a cell is placed in a solution with a high sugar concentration, the free water concentration is lower outside the cell than inside. Water moves out of the cell by osmosis until the concentrations equalise on both sides of the membrane.

subtopic.name: Osmotic regulation
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers osmosis as a special case of diffusion involving the movement of free water across a semi-permeable membrane. It also covers tonicity and how hypertonic, isotonic and hypotonic environments affect the volume of both animal and plant cells.
subtopic.why: Osmosis is essential for understanding how cells regulate their water content. Tonicity explains real-world phenomena such as why red blood cells burst in pure water, why plants wilt without water, and how kidney dialysis machines work.

items.title: I can define tonicity, hypertonic, isotonic and hypotonic
items.what: Tonicity describes how the concentration of solutes in an extracellular solution determines the direction and rate of osmosis, and therefore the volume of a cell. Hypotonic means the solution has a lower solute concentration than inside the cell. Isotonic means the same concentration. Hypertonic means a higher solute concentration than inside the cell.
items.why: Precise definitions of these terms are essential for explaining what happens to cells in different environments. Examiners expect you to define these relative to the cell's internal environment.
items.example: Distilled water is hypotonic relative to a red blood cell because it contains no solutes, whereas the cell's cytosol contains dissolved salts and proteins. The free water concentration is higher outside the cell.

subtopic.name: Osmotic regulation
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers osmosis as a special case of diffusion involving the movement of free water across a semi-permeable membrane. It also covers tonicity and how hypertonic, isotonic and hypotonic environments affect the volume of both animal and plant cells.
subtopic.why: Osmosis is essential for understanding how cells regulate their water content. Tonicity explains real-world phenomena such as why red blood cells burst in pure water, why plants wilt without water, and how kidney dialysis machines work.

items.title: I can distinguish between the movement of substances in hypertonic, isotonic and hypotonic environments for animal cells
items.what: In an isotonic solution, there is no net movement of water and the cell maintains its normal shape. In a hypertonic solution, water moves out of the cell by osmosis and the cell shrinks (crenation). In a hypotonic solution, water moves into the cell by osmosis and the cell swells and may burst (haemolysis, or lysis in other animal cells).
items.why: Knowing how animal cells respond to different environments is essential for understanding medical applications like saline drips and kidney dialysis, and for predicting outcomes in experimental scenarios.
items.example: A red blood cell placed in distilled water (hypotonic) will swell as water enters by osmosis. Eventually the cell bursts — this is called haemolysis. A red blood cell placed in concentrated salt water (hypertonic) will shrink as water leaves — this is called crenation.

subtopic.name: Osmotic regulation
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers osmosis as a special case of diffusion involving the movement of free water across a semi-permeable membrane. It also covers tonicity and how hypertonic, isotonic and hypotonic environments affect the volume of both animal and plant cells.
subtopic.why: Osmosis is essential for understanding how cells regulate their water content. Tonicity explains real-world phenomena such as why red blood cells burst in pure water, why plants wilt without water, and how kidney dialysis machines work.

items.title: I can distinguish between the movement of substances in hypertonic, isotonic and hypotonic environments for plant cells
items.what: In an isotonic solution, there is no net movement of water and the plant cell is in equilibrium. In a hypertonic solution, water moves out of the cell, the plasma membrane pulls away from the cell wall, and the cell becomes flaccid then plasmolysed. In a hypotonic solution, water moves into the cell, the vacuole expands, and the cell becomes turgid. Plant cells do not burst because the cell wall provides structural support.
items.why: Plant cells respond differently to animal cells because of their cell wall. Understanding these differences explains everyday observations like wilting flowers and is regularly assessed in VCE Biology.
items.example: A plant left unwatered is in a hypertonic environment relative to its cells. Water leaves the cells by osmosis, the vacuoles shrink, the plasma membrane pulls away from the cell wall (plasmolysis), and the plant wilts (becomes flaccid). Watering restores the hypotonic environment and the cells become turgid again.

subtopic.what: This subtopic covers osmosis as a special case of diffusion involving the movement of free water across a semi-permeable membrane. It also covers tonicity and how hypertonic, isotonic and hypotonic environments affect the volume of both animal and plant cells.
subtopic.why: Osmosis is essential for understanding how cells regulate their water content. Tonicity explains real-world phenomena such as why red blood cells burst in pure water, why plants wilt without water, and how kidney dialysis machines work.

items.title: I can determine the isotonic point from experimental data
items.what: The isotonic point is the concentration at which there is no net gain or loss of mass in a cell, because the solute concentration of the solution equals that inside the cell. On a graph of mass change versus solution concentration, the isotonic point is where the line crosses zero mass change.
items.why: This skill tests your ability to apply definitions of tonicity to interpret experimental data, which is a common exam question format in VCE Biology.
items.example: Apple pieces were placed in salt solutions of 0%, 0.5%, 2%, 5% and 10%. At 0% and 0.5% the pieces gained mass; at 2%, 5% and 10% they lost mass. The isotonic point is approximately 1%, because that is where the mass change crosses zero — no net movement of water in or out.

subtopic.why: Osmosis is essential for understanding how cells regulate their water content. Tonicity explains real-world phenomena such as why red blood cells burst in pure water, why plants wilt without water, and how kidney dialysis machines work.

items.title: I can define surface area to volume ratio and demonstrate how to calculate it
items.what: Surface area is the area of the plasma membrane exposed to the external environment. Volume is the space inside the cell (the cytoplasm). The SA:V ratio is calculated by dividing surface area by volume. For a cube: SA = 6l squared, V = l cubed.
items.why: Being able to calculate SA:V ratio allows you to compare the exchange efficiency of different-sized cells and to support your explanations with numerical evidence in assessments.
items.example: A cube with side length 1 has SA = 6, V = 1, so SA:V = 6:1. A cube with side length 3 has SA = 54, V = 27, so SA:V = 2:1. The smaller cube has three times the relative surface area available for exchange per unit of volume.

subtopic.name: Cell geometry and exchange
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how the surface area to volume ratio (SA:V) affects the efficiency of exchange across the plasma membrane. It explains why cell size is limited and identifies three ways cells can increase their SA:V ratio: flattened shape, compartments (organelles), and folds.
subtopic.why: SA:V ratio determines how efficiently a cell can exchange substances with its environment. This concept explains why cells divide when they grow too large and why different cell shapes and structures exist.

items.title: I can summarise the impact of changing SA:V ratio on the efficiency of cellular functions
items.what: As a cell grows, its volume increases faster than its surface area, so the SA:V ratio decreases. A lower SA:V ratio means less membrane surface is available per unit volume for exchanging nutrients and wastes, making exchange less efficient. Eventually, the cell cannot sustain itself and must divide.
items.why: This concept explains why cells are small, why they divide, and why large organisms need specialised organ systems for exchange rather than relying on diffusion alone.
items.example: A cell with a SA:V of 6:1 exchanges materials efficiently because every unit of volume has six units of surface for transport. If the cell doubles in size and the SA:V drops to 3:1, each unit of volume now has only half the surface area, so nutrients take longer to reach the centre.

subtopic.name: Cell geometry and exchange
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how the surface area to volume ratio (SA:V) affects the efficiency of exchange across the plasma membrane. It explains why cell size is limited and identifies three ways cells can increase their SA:V ratio: flattened shape, compartments (organelles), and folds.
subtopic.why: SA:V ratio determines how efficiently a cell can exchange substances with its environment. This concept explains why cells divide when they grow too large and why different cell shapes and structures exist.

items.title: I can identify the three ways cells increase their SA:V ratio
items.what: Cells can increase their SA:V ratio without increasing volume by having a flattened shape (thin, flat cells have higher SA:V than spherical cells of the same volume), compartments (membrane-bound organelles create additional internal surface area), and folds (folded membranes pack more surface into a smaller space).
items.why: These three strategies explain the diversity of cell shapes and structures observed in living organisms, and connect SA:V ratio to the earlier topic of organelles and compartmentalisation.
items.example: The cells lining the small intestine have tiny folds called villi and microvilli that increase the absorptive surface area by approximately 600-fold, giving a total surface area roughly the size of a tennis court. Root hair cells in plants use a similar strategy to maximise water absorption from soil.

subtopic.name: Cell geometry and exchange
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how the surface area to volume ratio (SA:V) affects the efficiency of exchange across the plasma membrane. It explains why cell size is limited and identifies three ways cells can increase their SA:V ratio: flattened shape, compartments (organelles), and folds.
subtopic.why: SA:V ratio determines how efficiently a cell can exchange substances with its environment. This concept explains why cells divide when they grow too large and why different cell shapes and structures exist.

items.title: I can give reasons why cell size is limited
items.what: As a cell grows, its SA:V ratio decreases because volume increases faster than surface area. Eventually, the plasma membrane cannot exchange nutrients and wastes fast enough to support the volume of the cell. The cell would be unable to maintain safe internal conditions and would die. This is why growing cells divide when they reach a certain size.
items.why: This is a key conceptual question in VCE Biology that requires you to link SA:V ratio, transport efficiency and cell survival into a logical sequence.
items.example: A very large cell would struggle to get enough oxygen to its centre by diffusion alone, because the distance from the membrane to the centre is too great. At the same time, waste products like CO2 would accumulate in the interior faster than they could be removed. The cell must divide to restore a higher SA:V ratio.

subtopic.why: SA:V ratio determines how efficiently a cell can exchange substances with its environment. This concept explains why cells divide when they grow too large and why different cell shapes and structures exist.

items.title: I can explain the function of chloroplasts
items.what: Chloroplasts are the organelles in plant and algal cells where photosynthesis occurs. They convert light energy into chemical energy by using carbon dioxide and water to produce glucose and oxygen. Autotrophs are organisms that make their own organic materials this way, while heterotrophs must consume other organisms.
items.why: Understanding the role of chloroplasts links organelle structure to function and explains why plants are the primary producers in most ecosystems.
items.example: A leaf cell contains many chloroplasts because its primary function is photosynthesis. A root cell, which is underground and receives no light, does not contain chloroplasts and relies on glucose transported from the leaves.

subtopic.name: Photosynthetic pathways
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the process of photosynthesis, including the word and balanced chemical equations, the structure of the chloroplast, and the locations of the light-dependent and light-independent stages. It also covers autotrophs and the role of chlorophyll.
subtopic.why: Photosynthesis is the process that converts light energy into chemical energy stored in glucose, providing the foundation for almost all food chains. Understanding it is essential for explaining how energy enters living systems.

items.title: I can draw a chloroplast and label its key structures and their functions
items.what: A chloroplast has a double membrane (outer and inner). Inside are grana (stacks of thylakoid membranes) where chlorophyll is located and the light-dependent stage occurs. The stroma is the gel-like fluid surrounding the grana, where the light-independent stage occurs. Chloroplasts also contain their own ribosomes and DNA, evidence of endosymbiosis.
items.why: Linking each structure to its function demonstrates deep understanding and is commonly assessed through diagram-based questions.
items.example: The thylakoid membranes are stacked into grana to maximise the surface area available for chlorophyll to capture light energy. More thylakoid membranes means more light can be absorbed and more photosynthesis can occur.

subtopic.name: Photosynthetic pathways
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the process of photosynthesis, including the word and balanced chemical equations, the structure of the chloroplast, and the locations of the light-dependent and light-independent stages. It also covers autotrophs and the role of chlorophyll.
subtopic.why: Photosynthesis is the process that converts light energy into chemical energy stored in glucose, providing the foundation for almost all food chains. Understanding it is essential for explaining how energy enters living systems.

items.title: I can state the word equation and balanced chemical equation for photosynthesis
items.what: Word equation: carbon dioxide + water (with light energy and chlorophyll) produces oxygen + glucose. Balanced chemical equation: 6CO2 + 6H2O (with light energy and chlorophyll) produces 6O2 + C6H12O6. Light energy and chlorophyll must be written above or below the arrow, not as reactants.
items.why: Accurate recall of these equations is directly assessed in VCE Biology. Writing light energy and chlorophyll in the correct position shows you understand they are conditions for the reaction, not reactants consumed.
items.example: A common error is writing light energy as a reactant on the left side of the equation. The correct format places 'light energy' above the arrow and 'chlorophyll' below the arrow, indicating both are required conditions for the reaction to proceed.

subtopic.name: Photosynthetic pathways
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the process of photosynthesis, including the word and balanced chemical equations, the structure of the chloroplast, and the locations of the light-dependent and light-independent stages. It also covers autotrophs and the role of chlorophyll.
subtopic.why: Photosynthesis is the process that converts light energy into chemical energy stored in glucose, providing the foundation for almost all food chains. Understanding it is essential for explaining how energy enters living systems.

items.title: I can summarise the inputs, outputs and location of the stages of photosynthesis
items.what: The light-dependent stage occurs on the thylakoid membranes (grana). It uses light energy and water, and produces oxygen. The light-independent stage occurs in the stroma. It uses carbon dioxide and produces glucose. Both stages are controlled by enzymes.
items.why: Being able to connect each stage to its location and its inputs and outputs is essential for answering multi-part exam questions about photosynthesis.
items.example: If you are asked where oxygen is produced during photosynthesis, the answer is the thylakoid membranes (grana) during the light-dependent stage. If asked where glucose is made, the answer is the stroma during the light-independent stage.

subtopic.name: Photosynthetic pathways
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the process of photosynthesis, including the word and balanced chemical equations, the structure of the chloroplast, and the locations of the light-dependent and light-independent stages. It also covers autotrophs and the role of chlorophyll.
subtopic.why: Photosynthesis is the process that converts light energy into chemical energy stored in glucose, providing the foundation for almost all food chains. Understanding it is essential for explaining how energy enters living systems.

items.title: I can explain the function of mitochondria
items.what: Mitochondria are the organelles where the second and third stages of aerobic cellular respiration occur (the Krebs cycle and the electron transport chain). They are known as the powerhouse of the cell because they produce the majority of ATP. All eukaryotic cells contain mitochondria.
items.why: Mitochondria link organelle structure to energy production. Understanding their role explains why cells with high energy demands, such as muscle cells, contain large numbers of mitochondria.
items.example: A cardiac (heart) muscle cell contains thousands of mitochondria because it contracts continuously and requires a constant supply of ATP. A skin cell, which is less metabolically active, contains far fewer.

subtopic.name: Glucose to ATP
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers aerobic and anaerobic cellular respiration, including glycolysis, the Krebs cycle and the electron transport chain. It covers the structure of the mitochondrion, the word equations for each pathway, and the comparison between aerobic and anaerobic respiration.
subtopic.why: Cellular respiration is how all cells release energy from glucose to make ATP. Understanding both aerobic and anaerobic pathways explains how organisms function under different conditions and why aerobic respiration is far more efficient.

items.title: I can draw a mitochondrion and label its key structures and their functions
items.what: A mitochondrion has a double membrane. The inner membrane is highly folded into cristae, which is the site of the electron transport chain and where most ATP is produced. The matrix is the fluid inside the inner membrane, where the Krebs cycle occurs. Mitochondria also have their own DNA and ribosomes, evidence of endosymbiosis.
items.why: Connecting each structure to the specific stage of respiration that occurs there is a key exam skill. The folded cristae also link back to SA:V ratio concepts.
items.example: The cristae are highly folded to maximise the surface area available for the electron transport chain, just as villi in the small intestine increase surface area for absorption. More cristae means more ATP can be produced.

subtopic.name: Glucose to ATP
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers aerobic and anaerobic cellular respiration, including glycolysis, the Krebs cycle and the electron transport chain. It covers the structure of the mitochondrion, the word equations for each pathway, and the comparison between aerobic and anaerobic respiration.
subtopic.why: Cellular respiration is how all cells release energy from glucose to make ATP. Understanding both aerobic and anaerobic pathways explains how organisms function under different conditions and why aerobic respiration is far more efficient.

items.title: I can summarise the inputs, outputs and location of the stages of aerobic cellular respiration
items.what: Glycolysis occurs in the cytosol: glucose is broken down into two pyruvate molecules, producing 2 ATP. It does not require oxygen. The Krebs cycle occurs in the matrix: pyruvate is further broken down, producing 2 ATP and CO2. The electron transport chain occurs on the cristae: oxygen is used, water is produced, and 32-34 ATP are generated.
items.why: Knowing the location, inputs and outputs of each stage allows you to answer detailed questions about what happens at each point in the process and to explain the overall equation.
items.example: If asked at which stage oxygen is used in aerobic cellular respiration, the answer is the electron transport chain on the cristae. If asked where carbon dioxide is produced, the answer is the Krebs cycle in the matrix.

subtopic.name: Glucose to ATP
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers aerobic and anaerobic cellular respiration, including glycolysis, the Krebs cycle and the electron transport chain. It covers the structure of the mitochondrion, the word equations for each pathway, and the comparison between aerobic and anaerobic respiration.
subtopic.why: Cellular respiration is how all cells release energy from glucose to make ATP. Understanding both aerobic and anaerobic pathways explains how organisms function under different conditions and why aerobic respiration is far more efficient.

items.title: I can state the word equation for aerobic cellular respiration
items.what: The word equation is: glucose + oxygen produces carbon dioxide + water + energy (ATP). The balanced chemical equation is: C6H12O6 + 6O2 produces 6CO2 + 6H2O + 36 or 38 ATP.
items.why: Accurate recall of this equation is directly assessed. Noting that this equation is essentially the reverse of photosynthesis helps you understand the complementary relationship between the two processes.
items.example: Photosynthesis uses CO2 and H2O to produce glucose and O2. Aerobic cellular respiration uses glucose and O2 to produce CO2 and H2O. The products of one process are the reactants of the other.

subtopic.name: Glucose to ATP
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers aerobic and anaerobic cellular respiration, including glycolysis, the Krebs cycle and the electron transport chain. It covers the structure of the mitochondrion, the word equations for each pathway, and the comparison between aerobic and anaerobic respiration.
subtopic.why: Cellular respiration is how all cells release energy from glucose to make ATP. Understanding both aerobic and anaerobic pathways explains how organisms function under different conditions and why aerobic respiration is far more efficient.

items.title: I can state the word equations for anaerobic cellular respiration and compare it to aerobic respiration
items.what: In plants and yeast (alcoholic fermentation): glucose produces ethanol + carbon dioxide + energy (2 ATP). In animals (lactic acid fermentation): glucose produces lactic acid + energy (2 ATP). Anaerobic respiration occurs entirely in the cytosol, produces only 2 ATP per glucose, and does not require oxygen.
items.why: Comparing aerobic and anaerobic pathways is a common exam question. Key differences include oxygen requirement, ATP yield, location and products.
items.example: Aerobic respiration produces 36-38 ATP per glucose molecule, whereas anaerobic respiration produces only 2 ATP. However, anaerobic respiration produces ATP more rapidly, which is why muscles use it during intense short bursts of exercise when oxygen supply cannot keep up with demand.

subtopic.name: Glucose to ATP
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers aerobic and anaerobic cellular respiration, including glycolysis, the Krebs cycle and the electron transport chain. It covers the structure of the mitochondrion, the word equations for each pathway, and the comparison between aerobic and anaerobic respiration.
subtopic.why: Cellular respiration is how all cells release energy from glucose to make ATP. Understanding both aerobic and anaerobic pathways explains how organisms function under different conditions and why aerobic respiration is far more efficient.

items.title: I can explain the structure of ATP and ADP and how energy is stored and released
items.what: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) consists of adenosine (adenine + ribose sugar) and three phosphate groups. When the bond between the second and third phosphate is broken, energy is released and ADP (adenosine diphosphate) is formed. When excess energy is available, a phosphate group is added back to ADP to reform ATP.
items.why: The ATP-ADP cycle is the fundamental mechanism by which cells store and release energy. Without this understanding, you cannot fully explain active transport, muscle contraction, or any energy-requiring cell process.
items.example: When a muscle cell contracts, ATP is broken down to ADP + Pi, releasing energy that powers the contraction. Later, during cellular respiration, the energy from breaking down glucose is used to reattach the phosphate to ADP, reforming ATP.

subtopic.name: Cellular energetics
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how energy flows through living systems, the structure and function of ATP as the energy currency of the cell, the ATP-ADP cycle (energy shuttle), and the distinction between autotrophs and heterotrophs.
subtopic.why: ATP is the molecule that directly powers almost all cellular processes. Understanding how it is made, used and recycled ties together photosynthesis, cellular respiration and active transport into a coherent picture of cell function.

items.title: I can demonstrate an understanding of why cells need ATP to survive
items.what: ATP is required for many essential cellular processes including active transport, cell growth and repair, muscle movement, nerve impulse transmission, protein synthesis, endocytosis and exocytosis. Cells cannot directly use the energy stored in glucose; they must first convert it to ATP through cellular respiration.
items.why: This concept links energy transformation to specific cell functions, explaining why disruption of ATP production (for example, by lack of oxygen) rapidly leads to cell death.
items.example: The sodium-potassium pump in a neuron requires ATP to move ions against their concentration gradient. Without ATP, the pump stops working, the ion gradient collapses, and the neuron can no longer transmit nerve impulses.

subtopic.name: Cellular energetics
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how energy flows through living systems, the structure and function of ATP as the energy currency of the cell, the ATP-ADP cycle (energy shuttle), and the distinction between autotrophs and heterotrophs.
subtopic.why: ATP is the molecule that directly powers almost all cellular processes. Understanding how it is made, used and recycled ties together photosynthesis, cellular respiration and active transport into a coherent picture of cell function.

items.title: I can distinguish between autotrophs and heterotrophs in terms of how they obtain energy
items.what: Autotrophs make their own organic materials by taking in energy from the environment. Green plants use light energy to convert CO2 and H2O into glucose through photosynthesis. Heterotrophs cannot make their own food and must consume other organisms to obtain organic materials, which they break down through cellular respiration to make ATP.
items.why: This distinction explains the flow of energy through ecosystems and connects photosynthesis and cellular respiration as complementary processes.
items.example: A grass plant is an autotroph: it uses sunlight to make glucose by photosynthesis, then uses that glucose in cellular respiration to produce ATP. A cow is a heterotroph: it eats the grass to obtain glucose, then carries out cellular respiration to make its own ATP.

items.title: I can explain the complementary relationship between photosynthesis and cellular respiration
items.what: The products of photosynthesis (glucose and oxygen) are the reactants of aerobic cellular respiration. The products of aerobic cellular respiration (carbon dioxide and water) are the reactants of photosynthesis. Photosynthesis occurs only during daylight in chloroplasts; cellular respiration occurs 24 hours a day in the cytosol and mitochondria.
items.why: Understanding this cycle explains how carbon, hydrogen and oxygen are continuously recycled through organisms and their environments, and why both processes are essential for life.
items.example: A plant in the dark only carries out cellular respiration, so it takes in O2 and releases CO2. In daylight, it carries out both processes, but photosynthesis occurs faster, so the plant has a net uptake of CO2 and a net release of O2. This is why measuring gas exchange alone does not prove respiration has stopped.
